series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes swap slot allocation by allocating contiguous slots in batches, reducing the number of small write requests and improving performance. It achieves this by recording the number of pages of each order that need a slot before swapping out a batch, and then making those allocations follow contiguous free slots. This approach helps to minimize the fragmentation of swap clusters and reduces the overhead of small write requests.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the patch does not address workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested further consideration for these use cases.

Reviewer noted that the patch does not apply its contiguous allocation heuristic to folios larger than a certain order, and found this omission reasonable.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern that the patch's preference for non-full clusters with contiguous slots may lead to increased lock contention, especially as swapfiles become more fragmented.

Reviewer Nhat Pham raised concerns about the effectiveness of the contiguous swap slot allocation heuristic, questioning whether it would lead to overshooting the estimate and creating problems down the line. They also suggested that this heuristic might not be necessary for cgroups that enable zswap or zram.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for looking into this! There are still workloads that benefit
more from disk swapping than compression swapping... We should make
the swap subsystem work for them.

I haven't read the code too closely, as it's an RFC meant to show the
general idea. So I'll just make some comments and ask some questions
about the idea:

---

Ah so we don't invoke this heuristics for folio larger than certain
orders? Makes sense.

---

So we prefer non-full clusters with contiguous slots, over free
clusters, over other nonfull clusters.

I think this part makes sense to me FWIW. We do skip fast path and go
for slow paths more often, so do make sure we're not paying with too
much lock contention, especially as the swapfile fils or get more
fragmented (which this patch series does nudge us towards). But FWIW,
we pretty much go back to the old behavior the moment we fail to find
contiguity for the first time in the batch, so I think we'll be
fine...?

---

Some general questions:

1. How many pages in folio_list typically do get reclaimed? There can
be quite a few with references, which we rotate/promote, when we scan,
right? Would constantly overshooting the estimate create problem down
the line?

(This is one of the few places where indirection (vswap) would have
helped - we can collect a batch of pages after unmapping, then pass
them to the phys swap allocator (after checking zswappability, etc.).
Maybe we can solve it better after it's landed, and accept an
imperfect solution for now?)

2. Should we skip this heuristics for cgroups that enables zswap (and
maybe zram)? Contiguity matters less there... unless it help at
writeback time? Hard to say without experimentation - maybe you can do
the same check you did for your zswap writeback batching patch series?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

review_comments.author: Mike Snitzer
review_comments.summary: The reviewer, Mike Snitzer, reviewed the sashiko review of the patch and found three issues that needed to be addressed in v9. He provided detailed explanations for each issue, including a folio being counted twice due to a stale dirty tag, NFSD not completing page-aligned edges inside a block, and a short write leaving a mark on a folio.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks, I've now trained my claude monkey with it. But I'm sure it'll
still throw feces periodically.

Also, I've reviewed the sashiko review of this v8, that you kindly
forwarded this morning, and 3 of the 7 issues it flagged were real.

I don't want to spam the lists more than I already have by immediately
posting v9... but it has needed changes, blech.  I'll at least wait to
see if Chuck picks up 1/7 to fold into the commit it fixes which is
already staged in cel/nfsd-testing (and if so I'll move Chuck and Jeff
to cc and upgrade -mm and -fsdevel to the To: for v9's posting...)

But here is the changelog for pending v9, in case it helps reviewers
side-step reporting something in v8 that is already addressed in v9:

Changes since v8, from the sashiko findings Jeff Layton relayed:
- 2/7 and 4/7: a folio is counted in WB_DONTCACHE_DIRTY only when both
  PG_dirty and its dirty tag are set.  v8 tested the tag alone.
  __folio_cancel_dirty() clears PG_dirty but leaves the tag, so a
  cancelled folio that stays cached kept a stale tag.  2/7 then
  uncounted such a folio twice, and 4/7 counted it and never uncounted
  it.
- 7/7: NFSD finds the edges a buffered segment shares by the mapping's
  smallest folio, as iomap does, not by page.  On 16 KiB blocks, a WRITE
  written as one buffered segment can have page-aligned ends inside a
  block.  Nothing completed those edges, and the folios stayed cached
  until reclaim.  NFSD also completes a segment's first edge only when
  the write reached the end of the segment's bytes in that unit.  A
  short write that stopped inside the unit had not written its part.
- 1/7 and 5/7: a paragraph each on a limit the review raised.  1/7
  cannot keep a larger cached folio, left by readahead, from spanning
  the cut.  5/7 marks the folio before iomap validates the iomap.  A
  stale iomap stopped by a fatal signal then leaves a mark on a folio
  this write did not complete.  Both cost one read-back and no data.
- 3/7 and 6/7: unchanged.

Longer form for the fixes that fell out from the v8 sashiko review:

2/7, the stale dirty tag: real.  __folio_cancel_dirty() uncounts a
dropbehind folio and clears PG_dirty, but leaves PAGECACHE_TAG_DIRTY
set.  Only writeback and truncation clear the tag, and writeback skips
a clean folio.  So a cancelled folio that stays cached keeps a stale
tag, and my clear path uncounted it a second time.  The same stale tag
made folio_mark_dropbehind() in 4/7 count a clean folio that nothing
would uncount.  v9 tests PG_dirty as well as the tag in both places.
A folio is counted only when both are set.  The race the tag closes
stays closed.  A dirtier that has set PG_dirty but not yet counted the
folio has not set the tag either.

7/7, the PAGE_SIZE edge tests: real.  On 16 KiB blocks, a WRITE written
as one buffered segment can have page-aligned ends inside a block.
iomap left those edges for NFSD to complete, and NFSD never asked about
them.  Those folios stayed cached until reclaim.  v9 finds the edges by the
mapping's smallest folio, as iomap does.  Measured on the loop device,
whose dma_alignment of 511 makes every TCP payload memory-misaligned.
NFSD then writes each WRITE as one buffered segment.  32 writers of
12288-byte records: v8 left all 32,736 pages of a 128 MiB file
resident.  v9 leaves 1,348 of 262,080 pages of a 1 GiB file, 0.5%.

7/7, the short write that completes the first edge: real, and the cost
is one read-back on the retry.  v9 completes the first edge only when
the write reached the end of the segment's bytes in that unit.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm/huge_memory: scale thp_underused() to the folio size
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the thp_underused() function to be aware of the size of a folio, rather than assuming it's always PMD-sized. It scales the khugepaged_max_ptes_none threshold proportionally to the number of pages in the folio, ensuring that the same fraction of zero-filled pages is tolerated regardless of folio size. This change will prevent issues when collapsing mTHP orders and splitting folios, as both operations would use the same threshold for a given folio size. The patch makes no functional changes for PMD-sized folios, as their nr_pages value remains HPAGE_PMD_NR.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm/huge_memory: don't queue folios when underused splitting is inactive
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of anonymous PMD-sized folios by skipping their queueing when underused splitting is inactive, which is the default case due to the maximum value of khugepaged/max_ptes_none. This change reduces unnecessary work and improves system performance. The patch introduces a new function thp_underused_never() that checks if underused splitting is never performed based on the sysctl value. It also updates the deferred_split_folio() function to use this new check. This optimization has implications for subsequent patches, including one that adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, allowing them to be split and reclaimed when under memory pressure. This is necessary because without this change, fully mapped mTHP folios that are mostly zero-filled would not get split by the deferred split shrinker, leading to memory regressions. The patch mirrors the existing behavior for PMD-sized folios and only queues mTHP folios of at least 2M for underused splitting. This is a conservative approach to minimize overhead on the common order-0 fault path.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory regressions caused by 2M THP=always on arm64 by allowing the underused shrinker to handle anonymous mTHP folios. The patches modify the thp_underused() function to be size-aware, prevent unnecessary queuing of folios for splitting when underused shrinking is inactive, and add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list with a minimum size of 2M.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/2] memcg: reduce cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists
series_items.patch_summary: This patch reduces cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists by rearranging the layout of struct mem_cgroup_per_node in memory. The goal is to minimize unnecessary cache line sharing, which can lead to increased lock contention and performance degradation. Specifically, it moves the 'memcg_pn_cold' group, which is only accessed during memcg reparenting or freeing, to be adjacent to the 'memcg_pn_read_mostly' group, allowing these two groups to share a cacheline instead of the LRU list heads. This change improves performance in multi-threaded workloads with high memory access rates.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] memcg: don't go through the lruvec for folio and kmem lruvec stat updates
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the update of per-memcg LRU statistics by bypassing the lruvec lookup and instead passing the memcg and node directly to mod_memcg_node_state(). This reduces contention on a shared cacheline, improving throughput in certain workloads. The change is made in the mm/memcontrol.c file and affects the reparent_memcg_lruvec_state_local() function. The patch was submitted by Joanne Koong and has been acknowledged by Shakeel Butt.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to reduce cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists by rearranging the struct mem_cgroup_per_node layout and modifying the folio and kmem lruvec stat updates. The goal is to improve performance on CPUs with spatial prefetching, such as Intel CPUs.

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Mentioned a limitation of the current slab layout that may affect the measured performance improvement. Noted it's not a correctness issue, but rather a potential optimization opportunity.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, 23 Oct 2026 12:54:15 -0700 Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:

> Memcg lruvec stat updates read fields of struct mem_cgroup_per_node and struct
> lruvec that can share a 128-byte cacheline pair with lines the lru_lock holder
> writes constantly (the LRU list heads, lru_lock or lru_zone_size[]), depending
> on where struct mem_cgroup_per_node lands in its slab. On CPUs that do spatial
> prefetching (eg Intel CPUs), this makes the stat updates contend with the
> lru_lock holder.
> 
> Patch 1 rearranges struct mem_cgroup_per_node so that its read-mostly line is
> paired with a cold line, and patch 2 makes the folio and kmem stat updates use
> the memcg and node they already know instead of going through the lruvec,
> whose pgdat field shares a cacheline pair with lru_lock or lru_zone_size[].
> 
> Results on a 2-socket Skylake (80 CPUs), average pages per second for
> threads faulting in and freeing memory in a single memcg:
> 
> 	   base     patch 1   patch 1+2 
> shmem, 20 threads  4.74M    5.59M     5.77M
> shmem, 80 threads  7.94M    8.66M     8.82M
> anon,  20 threads  3.04M    3.08M     3.10M

Thanks.  A local AI review pointed out a thing:

  One limitation worth mentioning in the [1/2] changelog: the slab
  uses SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN, which need not align each object to a
  128-byte boundary.  If an object starts 64 bytes into such a pair,
  its first line can still be paired with the end of the preceding
  object rather than its own cold line.  This isn't a correctness
  issue, and the measured Skylake improvement may well be real, but the
  layout doesn't guarantee that every read-mostly line pairs with a
  cold line.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v1] mm: move LRU size stat updates out of lru_lock in folio batches

version_history.subject: [PATCH v1] mm: move LRU size stat updates out of lru_lock in folio batches

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch moves the updates to LRU size statistics out of the lru_lock critical section in folio batches, reducing contention and improving performance. The stats are accumulated while holding the lock and applied after dropping it, resulting in at most one update per LRU list per batch. This change is expected to improve throughput by reducing the time spent waiting for the lru_lock and making the code more efficient.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that moving LRU size stat updates out of lru_lock improves throughput and agreed to restructure in v2 to address reviewer's concerns.

Author analyzed a perf profile run on her patch and found that while stat updates are only 0.7% of total cycles, lock contention from callers waiting for the lru_lock is still hurting throughput.

Author addressed Shakeel Butt's concern that removing LRU stat updates from lru_lock would not improve throughput, citing measurements showing similar performance with and without the patch.

Author acknowledges that moving LRU size stat updates out of lru_lock in folio batches may not have a significant impact on throughput, citing experiments and benchmark results. She plans to investigate further, specifically looking into page cache stats.
sentiment_signals: identified a need for further optimization
review_comments.raw_body:
Will do in v2. THe relevant part of [1] is that a change that added
just a few instructions to the memcg stat update path cost about 2%
throughput because the LRU stat updates run under lru_lock and the
overhead went away once they were moved outside of the lock, which is
what motivated this patch.

---

The perf profile run on the top commit of mm-new (commit fcec4f4bcc
"riscv: mm: fix concurrency in mark_new_valid_map()) using the same
benchmark setup (80 threads, shmem) shows:
- 52.8% of all cycles are spent spinning on the lru_lock (evenly split
between folio_batch_move_lru() and folios_put_refs())
- About 25% of the time spent holding lru_lock in those 2 paths goes
to the LRU stat updates (the ones this patch moves to outside the
lock) and the rest is the list manipulation itself
- Most of the cost in __mod_memcg_lruvec_state() is cache misses
(loading pn->memcg, pn->lruvec_stats_percpu, and the per-cpu
counters).

The stat updates are only 0.7% of total cycles but I think it's the
lock contention on callers waiting for the lock that ends up hurting
throughput.

---

With the LRU stat updates removed from these paths entirely, I'm
seeing that throughput is essentially the same as with this patch
(within noise):

                       mm-new   this patch   no stat updates
    shmem, 80 threads  7.94M    10.33M       10.31M
    anon,  20 threads  3.04M     3.35M        3.33M

I think once the updates are moved out of the critical section
entirely, they don't cost much to do.

---

I had experimented a little with doing this for LRU size stats in the
reclaim paths in vmscan and deferring the count_memcg_events() calls
in the same batch paths, but none of them made a measurable difference
to throughput. For the reclaim paths, I think it's because there
reclaim rather than the lru_lock is the bottleneck, and my benchmark

From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
Subject: [PATCH v4] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

Since commit 7e8756d7ad22 ("mm: page_alloc: fix non-movable reclaim
storm in defrag_mode"), direct reclaim and compaction for non-movable
requests under defrag_mode run at pageblock_order, to produce the whole
blocks that ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT needs. The retry decisions that follow
still use the request order. An order-0 request can therefore retry
indefinitely without ever reaching the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT fallback:

- Reclaim at pageblock_order gives up after one pass as soon as a zone
  looks compaction_ready(), and do_try_to_free_pages() then returns 1
  even though nothing was reclaimed. It returns before the retry that
  would reclaim memory.low-protected cgroups, so when most memory is
  protected, the pass that did run finds next to nothing.

- Compaction at pageblock_order fails or is deferred.

- should_reclaim_retry() takes the reported progress as progress for
  the order-0 request and resets no_progress_loops. The request
  retries.

Order 1-3 requests loop the same way, and should_compact_retry() also
checks their pageblock_order compaction result against the request
order.

On a production host (64G, defrag_mode, memory.low covering most of the
workload), 95% of direct reclaim runs were order-9 runs that returned 1
with nothing reclaimed, at up to 60k runs per second. Across ~200M
should_reclaim_retry() calls in a day, no_progress_loops never left 0.
The spinning allocations were SLUB slab refills for inode and dentry
caches. The time spent registers as memory pressure, and pressure-based
OOM killing takes down both workloads and system services.

For promoted requests:

- Reclaim progress does not reset no_progress_loops, as for costly
  orders.

- should_compact_retry() checks the compaction result at the promoted
  order and does not retry COMPACT_SKIPPED, since the request can fall
  back. The compaction priority floor and the COMPACT_SUCCESS retry
  limit stay those of the request order, so a non-costly request still
  gets its COMPACT_PRIO_SYNC_FULL pass before it falls back.

When a promoted request takes the fallback, reset the retry counters,
so that the fallback attempt gets a full retry budget before the OOM
killer is considered. A request whose reclaim was not promoted spent
its budget on the request itself and keeps its counters, as Usama Arif
pointed out.

__alloc_pages_slowpath() computes the promoted order once per iteration
and keeps it in alloc_context for direct reclaim, direct compaction and
the two retry helpers, so no callee has to recompute it. Harry Yoo asked
for the promoted order to be explicit rather than derived in each
callee, and Vlastimil Babka suggested alloc_context over new function
parameters.

In a VM reproducer (32G, defrag_mode, inode churn under memory.low):

                                        before    after
    should_reclaim_retry() calls           63M     293k
    peak memory pressure (PSI some avg10)  99%      12%

File creation runs 5.7x faster.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Assisted-by: LLM
Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>

>   would reclaim memory.low-protected cgroups, so when most memory is
>   protected, the pass that did run finds next to nothing.
> 
> - Compaction at pageblock_order fails or is deferred.
> 
> - should_reclaim_retry() takes the reported progress as progress for
>   the order-0 request and resets no_progress_loops. The request
>   retries.
>

> checks their pageblock_order compaction result against the request
> order.

> storm in defrag_mode"), direct reclaim and compaction for non-movable
> requests under defrag_mode run at pageblock_order, to produce the whole
> blocks that ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT needs. The retry decisions that follow
> still use the request order. An order-0 request can therefore retry
> indefinitely without ever reaching the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT fallback:
> 
> - Reclaim at pageblock_order gives up after one pass as soon as a zone
>   looks compaction_ready(), and do_try_to_free_pages() then returns 1
>   even though nothing was reclaimed. It returns before the retry that
>   would reclaim memory.low-protected cgroups, so when most memory is
>   protected, the pass that did run finds next to nothing.
> 
> - Compaction at pageblock_order fails or is deferred.
> 
> - should_reclaim_retry() takes the reported progress as progress for
>   the order-0 request and resets no_progress_loops. The request
>   retries.
> 
> Order 1-3 requests loop the same way, and should_compact_retry() also
> checks their pageblock_order compaction result against the request
> order.
> 
> On a production host (64G, defrag_mode, memory.low covering most of the
> workload), 95% of direct reclaim runs were order-9 runs that returned 1
> with nothing reclaimed, at up to 60k runs per second. Across ~200M
> should_reclaim_retry() calls in a day, no_progress_loops never left 0.
> The spinning allocations were SLUB slab refills for inode and dentry
> caches. The time spent registers as memory pressure, and pressure-based
> OOM killing takes down both workloads and system services.
> 
> For promoted requests:

> - Reclaim progress does not reset no_progress_loops, as for costly
>   orders.
> 
> - should_compact_retry() checks the compaction result at the promoted
>   order and does not retry COMPACT_SKIPPED, since the request can fall
>   back. The compaction priority floor and the COMPACT_SUCCESS retry
>   limit stay those of the request order, so a non-costly request still
>   gets its COMPACT_PRIO_SYNC_FULL pass before it falls back.
> 
> When a promoted request takes the fallback, reset the retry counters,
> so that the fallback attempt gets a full retry budget before the OOM
> killer is considered. A request whose reclaim was not promoted spent
> its budget on the request itself and keeps its counters, as Usama Arif
> pointed out.
> 
> __alloc_pages_slowpath() computes the promoted order once per iteration
> and keeps it in alloc_context for direct reclaim, direct compaction and
> the two retry helpers, so no callee has to recompute it. Harry Yoo asked
> for the promoted order to be explicit rather than derived in each
> callee, and Vlastimil Babka suggested alloc_context over new function
> parameters.
>

>     should_reclaim_retry() calls           63M     293k
>     peak memory pressure (PSI some avg10)  99%      12%
>
